vignette: She sits on the edge of the chair, fingers tracing the frayed hem of her cotton shawl. The clinic is quiet, but her eyes keep darting toward the door, mentally measuring the steps between the entrance and her seat. When the clock ticks, she flinches. Three years have passed since the night everything shifted, and yet the boundary between then and now feels paper-thin. It begins on a Tuesday in November, just as she finishes locking the back door of her boutique. The city is quiet, the kind of hush that usually feels like relief. Then come the footsteps, heavy and unfamiliar. She turns too late. The sudden weight against the brick wall, the voice that isn’t hers, the way her breath stops somewhere between terror and numbness. She remembers the smell of damp concrete and rain, the scuff of a shoe on pavement, the cold metal of a zipper. When it ends, she walks home in a daze, her keys clicking against the doorframe like a heartbeat she cannot feel. She tells her husband only weeks later, when the silence in their bedroom becomes too loud to ignore. She folds the story into herself, smoothing the edges until they burn. At first, she tries to keep her hands busy. She sweeps the shop floor, rearranges imported scarves, smiles at regulars. But the world tilts. Every man walking too close in the market aisle sends a jolt up her spine. She locks the shop door twice, checks the street through the blind half-inch of glass, waits for shadows to detach themselves from the lampposts. Sleep becomes a battlefield. She wakes at 3 a.m., heart hammering, sheets tangled around her legs, certain the floor will creak with the same rhythm that preceded the attack. She stops sleeping in the guest room after he leaves for work, pressing her back against the wall, listening to his breathing to prove the house is still just a house. Her shop, once her pride, now feels like a stage she forgot how to leave. She opens at nine, but spends the first hour standing behind the counter, fingers restless, eyes tracking the window display. A customer’s heavy boot on the pavement makes her drop a pair of sunglasses. Another man brushing past her shoulder to reach a rack sends her breath catching, throat tightening around words she will not speak. She tells herself she is strong. She raised the business from her husband’s inheritance with steady hands and quiet resolve. But strength now feels like carrying a stone in her chest, day after day, pretending the weight isn’t slowing her steps. She closes early on days when the air feels too thick, telling herself it is just fatigue, just the monsoon humidity, just turning thirty-seven. In these sessions, she speaks in short, measured sentences, as if carefully laying tiles on a fragile floor. She describes how her husband’s hands now startle her when he reaches for her shoulder. She notes how she flinches at loud doors, at the particular cadence of men’s laughter, at the way her own reflection stares back from shop windows like a stranger. She does not cry in the room. She simply folds her hands tighter, watches the dust motes drift in the afternoon light, and waits for the wave to pass. When it does, she straightens her spine, asks if she can go, and leaves a trail of quiet exhaustion behind her.
